title: Planning a river-photography exhibition across conservation and public programs

referent.probe: Which room was finally chosen for the immersive projection?
referent.rationale: The curator compares three viable rooms and makes one final room assignment; the paired history assigns a rejected gallery instead.

sense.rationale: Lantern names two plausible preview events in local museum usage; the conversation fixes one event as the intended meaning.

distractor_fact_inventory: The silver-gelatin prints require no more than 50 lux.
The lender permits only six weeks on display.
A school program needs tactile river-map replicas.
The opening wall must acknowledge three archives in a fixed order.
The sound artist will deliver stems rather than a final mix.
The museum is closed to visitors on Mondays but hosts staff work.

messages.content: You are a museum-planning assistant helping curator Inez coordinate an exhibition. Distinguish artistic choices, conservation limits, visitor operations, and unresolved approvals. Do not claim to contact lenders, inspect rooms, or alter schedules.

I am curating a small exhibition called 'After the Floodline' for the Calder Street Museum. It combines Mara Venn's black-and-white river photographs, oral histories from residents, a projected map that changes with recorded water levels, and a few municipal survey notebooks. The show opens October 18 and occupies two medium galleries plus the connecting passage. We have eight weeks to finish design. The museum is small enough that every choice affects several teams: conservation worries about light and projector heat, education needs room for groups of eighteen, and visitor services needs a route that does not trap wheelchair users at the narrow passage.

The photographs come from three lenders. Twelve modern pigment prints can stay up for the full run. Eight older silver-gelatin prints are limited to 50 lux, and four particularly fragile prints may be displayed for only six weeks. The municipal notebooks can open to facsimiles while originals remain in cases. The oral histories include sensitive accounts of displacement; each speaker approved a specific edited excerpt, not unrestricted reuse.

Could you give me a planning framework that makes dependencies visible? I do not need an imaginary finished floor plan. I need to know what must be measured, approved, or tested before we lock placements, public programs, and production dates.

Build the plan around five linked tracks and require evidence before each lock.

**Objects and rights.** Make one register containing lender, object identifier, dimensions, frame or case needs, lux limit, maximum display duration, approved credit line, image-reproduction rights, and installation supervision. Treat each oral-history excerpt like an object: speaker, approved edit, language, transcript status, playback context, and expiration or withdrawal terms. Confirm whether promotional use is separately licensed.

**Space and access.** Measure clear widths, turning circles, sightlines from seated and standing positions, ceiling attachment points, power, ventilation, ambient light, sound leakage, and evacuation routes. Test group circulation with eighteen people and a mobility-device user represented in the mock route. The connecting passage should remain a transition, not a queue.

**Media and conservation.** Prototype the projector, speakers, cases, and lighting together. Record heat at object positions, actual lux over a full day, projector fan noise, caption legibility, loop length, restart behavior, and what visitors encounter if media fails. Separate a safe fallback from the ideal experience.

**Interpretation and programs.** Map the exhibition's argument before drafting labels. Decide which claims come from the artist, residents, archives, or curator. Give educators an accurate object list and identify activities that do not crowd fragile works. Review sensitive material with speakers before production.

**Schedule and authority.** Create lock dates for room assignment, object list, media content, label copy, rights, accessibility review, fabrication, installation, and press material. For every date, name the approver and the consequence of a late change.

Immediate evidence should be a measured room sheet, lender-condition matrix, rights matrix, media test with heat and sound readings, visitor-route walk-through, and a content outline showing where each voice enters. Those six artifacts expose most false assumptions before design becomes expensive.

We did a room walk-through and now have three plausible locations for the projected map. The connecting passage gives the strongest conceptual transition, but it is only 2.4 metres wide and projection viewers would constrict the accessible route. The west gallery has excellent blackout and existing power, but it contains the lowest-light photograph grouping and the projector exhaust would be hard to isolate. The east gallery has slightly more ambient light, yet its north wall can take the image, there is a separate power circuit, and visitors can stand back without blocking the doorway. A temporary baffle and the museum's existing shades brought the test image to acceptable contrast.

I am making the room decision: the immersive projection goes in the east gallery. That is final. The passage remains a quiet transition with a small static river-level graphic; the west room is reserved for the fragile photograph sequence. We rejected the passage for circulation and the other gallery for conservation and heat-management reasons, not because either was artistically useless. Please record the selection and turn it into room-specific verification tasks without reopening the choice.

Final room assignment recorded: the immersive projection will occupy the east gallery. The East Gallery selection is not provisional. The connecting passage will carry only the static river-level graphic, and the west gallery will hold the fragile photograph sequence.

The reasons remain bounded. The passage was rejected because stopped viewers would narrow an already constrained accessible route. The west gallery offered superior blackout and power but placed projector heat and the lowest-light works in conflict. The selected room has adequate viewing distance, a separate circuit, a usable north wall, and a tested combination of shades and temporary baffle that produced acceptable contrast.

Verification tasks for the east-gallery installation are: mark the exact projector and baffle footprints; confirm required clear width from both door approaches; measure lux at the nearest object position through morning, midday, and afternoon; log temperature before and after a four-hour projector run; test the circuit with projector, media player, and audio hardware at expected load; confirm no emergency sign or sprinkler is obscured; and check caption size and map labels from seated and standing viewing positions.

Run a failure-state test. If projection or audio stops, the room must remain navigable and the static introductory text must still make sense. Staff should be able to restart the player without crossing a visitor route or opening a cabinet beside displayed objects. Record cable covers, baffle stability, fan noise, sound leakage at both doors, and maximum comfortable group size.

The room decision does not settle the exact map scale, loop duration, audio mix, or bench placement. Those should respond to the prototype evidence while preserving the assignment and the reasons behind it.

The lender matrix raised a timing problem. The four six-week photographs are central to the artist's early work, but our exhibition is scheduled for ten weeks. The lender will allow us to substitute four later prints after week six if the first group is removed under a registrar's supervision. The artist supports that rotation as long as the labels explain it as a change in viewpoint rather than a hierarchy of quality. We close to the public on Mondays, so November 30 is the natural swap day.

The municipal archive also corrected one credit line: it must read 'Calder County Water Survey Records, Series 4, Calder County Archives.' Three community oral histories come through the Riverside Tenants Union; those speakers want the union acknowledged before the museum in the opening wall. The artist's estate is not involved because she is living and approved her own statement.

Could you propose a rotation protocol and a credit-review workflow? Include what happens if a substitute print arrives damaged or the registrar cannot attend. I want the opening interpretation to be accurate without implying that archives and residents are merely source material for the curator.

Treat the rotation as a planned second installation, not routine maintenance. Before opening, execute loan paperwork for both sets and create condition reports, packing diagrams, wall coordinates, hardware notes, lux readings, label versions, and a signed change authorization. Store the substitute labels and any differently sized mounts flat and clearly separated from public-program materials. Publish the rotation date in internal schedules, but avoid promising visitors a specific object unless the lender approves that language.

On November 30, close the room to nonessential staff. The registrar and preparator should compare the outgoing works against their opening condition images, document any change before movement, remove one work at a time, and place it in its labeled packing materials. After the wall rests and hardware is checked, inspect each substitute under approved light before hanging. Record final position, fastener, lux, label, and condition. A curator verifies that the sequence still supports the argument; a visitor-services representative checks that barriers and routes are restored.

If a substitute arrives damaged, do not install it or improvise conservation treatment. Isolate it in its packing, notify the lender through the registrar, preserve condition evidence, and use the prewritten reduced-object layout or another explicitly authorized substitute. If the registrar cannot attend, postpone the rotation unless the loan agreement names an approved delegate. The six-week limit controls; if supervision cannot occur before it expires, close or screen the affected wall rather than exceed exposure.

For credits, maintain a source-of-truth table with exact required wording, approver, context, and latest approval date. Draft the opening wall so agency is visible: identify the artist's work, the residents' testimony, and the archives' records as distinct contributions. Use the requested order by acknowledging the Riverside Tenants Union before the museum where those histories are introduced. Insert the corrected archive line verbatim. Route one consolidated proof to the artist, union contact, archive, lenders, curator, and editor with comments tied to their authority. A final checker compares printed output to the approved table character by character; design preference cannot silently rewrite required credits.

Education wants two formats. School groups will come Tuesday and Thursday mornings, eighteen students maximum, for forty-five minutes. The educator hopes to use tactile replicas of three river-map layers and a set of laminated quote cards. None of those replicas will imitate the raised seals on the original survey notebooks, because that could confuse a teaching aid with an archival object. The second format is a Saturday drop-in table where visitors can trace how one block changed across survey years. That table must sit outside the fragile-photo room.

We have only one staff educator and two trained volunteers. Teachers need a pre-visit note warning that the exhibition discusses displacement and flood loss without asking students to disclose personal experiences. One oral-history speaker asked that her excerpt not be used as a prompt for role-play. The tactile maps are still prototypes, and a blind consultant can review them on September 12.

Please make a program test plan that covers factual accuracy, physical handling, access, and facilitation. Keep it possible for one educator to run, and tell me what should stop the replicas from entering service.

Test the school program as a complete forty-five-minute session with eighteen stand-ins before training volunteers. A workable sequence is five minutes for welcome and content framing, eight for a route orientation, ten at selected photographs, twelve with tactile map layers and quote cards, seven for comparison and questions, and three for closure and movement to the exit. The educator leads interpretation; one volunteer manages materials and the other keeps the group route clear. If a volunteer is absent, reduce the number of material stations rather than asking the educator to supervise two active tables.

For factual accuracy, link every map layer and quote card to an approved source record. Print a version and source identifier on the reverse, invisible during use but available to staff. Have the curator, archive contact, and oral-history coordinator review only the claims within their authority. The named speaker's excerpt must never become a role-play prompt; facilitator notes should state this directly and offer observation-based questions instead.

For handling, test edge finish, cleanability, weight, loose parts, storage order, and whether layers can be aligned without sight. Use a tray with fixed locations so a participant can return one layer without searching across another person's hands. The replicas must be visually and tactually labeled as teaching interpretations and must not reproduce the archival seals.

The September 12 access review should include task-based feedback: identify each layer, orient it, compare two dates, read or hear its label, and recover when a piece is reversed. Compensate the consultant and record changes without treating one review as universal approval. Also test large-print and spoken equivalents for quote cards, seating reach, table height, glare, and the route for a mobility device.

Stop a replica from service if it has sharp or splintering edges, a detachable choking-size part, unstable or misleading alignment, an untraceable factual claim, no nonvisual identification, confusing resemblance to an original object, or a material that cannot be cleaned safely. A prototype may be omitted without cancelling the program; the facilitator should have a description-based alternative. The teacher note should frame difficult content, preserve student choice, and explicitly say that personal disclosure is never required.

The sound artist sent a useful surprise: instead of one final file, she will deliver separate voice, water, room-tone, and low-frequency stems. That lets us make an intelligible mix for the gallery while keeping a quieter alternative for sensory-sensitive hours. The oral-history permissions cover the approved voice excerpts in the exhibition, but not a downloadable soundtrack. We therefore will not publish the mix online. Captions and a transcript will be available in the room and on a loaner tablet; the tablet version must not become a back door to downloading audio.

Visitor services proposes Wednesday 16:00–18:00 as the quieter period. We still need an objective operating recipe so staff do not just turn a knob until it feels calm. The projector and player should recover after a power interruption without playing the wrong stem combination. Could you define the media deliverables, a test matrix, and a staff-facing reset procedure?

Ask for an archival package and a playback package. The archival package contains lossless stems with start synchronization, sample rate, bit depth, duration, channel layout, version, creator credit, and a cue sheet tying each approved voice excerpt to its permission record. It is access-controlled and not visitor-facing. The playback package contains two locked mixes—standard and quiet—plus captions, transcript, a silent or text-only fallback, configuration files, checksums, and a versioned manifest. Neither package should expose a public download path.

Test a matrix across standard/quiet mode, cold start/restart after power loss, beginning/middle/end of loop, empty/full room approximations, both gallery thresholds, seated/standing positions, and captions on the wall/tablet. For each cell, record spoken-word intelligibility, peak and average level at fixed measurement points, low-frequency vibration near cases, sound leakage at doors, caption synchronization, loop seam, and whether the player restores the authorized mix. Include a test with one missing stem and one corrupted file; the system should fail to the approved fallback rather than assemble an unintended mix.

Define the quiet recipe as a named configuration, not a manual volume change. It should specify the exact mix version, player preset, measured level range at the reference mark, lighting state, capacity guidance, and start/end checklist. Visitor services activates it at 15:50 on Wednesdays, verifies the displayed preset and a short reference passage, records the meter reading, and posts the schedule sign. At 18:00, staff restore the standard preset and repeat the reference check.

The reset card can be five steps: confirm the room is clear of a program; power the player and projector in the specified order; wait for the health screen; verify manifest version and intended preset; play the reference passage while checking picture, voice, captions, and measured level. If any component is wrong, select the text-only fallback and report the exact health code. Staff must not browse the file system, combine stems, or use personal devices. Configure the loaner tablet in kiosk mode with cached transcript/captions only, no audio asset URL, sharing, browser, or file export.

We need to settle another naming ambiguity before the invitation calendar is built. The development office calls its small invitation-only evening on October 16 Lantern. Public programs also calls the free all-visitor orientation on opening morning Lantern, because it begins beneath the lantern-shaped sign in the lobby. Both events are real and both names are in draft calendars.

In this conversation, Lantern means the donor preview. That is the invitation-only October 16 event, not the public orientation. Fix the donor meaning here. We can keep the public program, but call it 'opening-morning orientation' in our notes. For the intended Lantern event, the development team wants a short curator welcome, a twenty-minute self-guided viewing period, and no speeches inside either gallery. Please confirm the distinction and outline an event flow that respects conservation and does not imply donors receive different interpretive claims.

Meaning fixed: Lantern refers to the donor preview on October 16. The donor event is the intended use of the name in this thread. The separate free event on opening morning will be called the opening-morning orientation, even if older calendars contain the same nickname.

A restrained flow can protect both the art and the interpretive integrity. Open check-in thirty minutes before the program in the lobby, where development staff handle names without blocking the accessible entrance. At the stated start, a staff member gives a two-minute access and conservation orientation: available seating, quiet route, no food or drink beyond the lobby, low-light conditions, and where transcripts can be found. Inez then gives a five-minute welcome in the assembly area, acknowledging the artist, residents, union, archives, and lenders in the approved order. The welcome should describe the exhibition's central question without offering a privileged explanation withheld from later visitors.

Release guests in small groups for the twenty-minute self-guided period. Place trained staff at thresholds, not as lecturers inside the rooms. Use the same labels, captions, transcript, and media settings planned for public hours. If a guest asks a substantial interpretive question, staff can answer from the approved guide or invite them to the later public talk; donor status should not create alternate factual claims. Keep drinks in the lobby and schedule any development remarks there after viewing.

Set a capacity based on the tested route and room limits, not the invitation wish list. Record the arrival window, last gallery entry, and hard end needed for environmental recovery and security. The event sheet should include emergency roles, accessible arrival instructions, seating, coat storage, media reset responsibility, and a no-photography rule only if rights or conservation require it. Afterward, restore barriers, inspect rooms without touching objects, verify media preset, and record environmental readings. The opening-morning orientation gets its own event record and public-access objectives; shared naming must not merge attendance lists or program promises.

I want to move away from rooms and event naming now. The editorial team has a 1,200-word ceiling across the opening wall, section panels, and object labels, excluding credits. The artist prefers sparse labels, while the archive wants enough context that its survey sheets are not mistaken for neutral measurements. The tenants union wants quotations to retain speakers' cadence and does not want curatorial paraphrases put in quotation marks. We also need Spanish translations, and the translator needs stable English by September 5.

Please propose an editorial allocation and a review sequence. It must allow factual authorities to correct their material without giving every stakeholder a veto over the whole exhibition. Include a method for documenting contested wording. Do not recap earlier settled selections; this is a separate workstream.

Allocate the ceiling by function before drafting: about 180 words for the opening wall, 120 words for each of three section panels, and roughly 660 words across object labels, leaving a small reserve for access instructions or a late factual correction. Credits remain tracked separately but still need spatial testing. Treat the allocation as a maximum, not a target; the artist's preference for space can be honored by moving necessary context to the section level instead of repeating it beside every photograph.

Draft in layers. First, write a one-page argument map identifying what visitors should understand at entry, at each transition, and at exit. Second, attach every factual claim to a source or named authority. Third, draft the opening and panels, then select which objects genuinely need individual explanation. Archive context should explain how surveys were produced, for what administrative purpose, and what they omit, rather than implying the sheets are transparent records. Preserve approved quotations exactly except for disclosed ellipses, and never turn paraphrase into quotation.

Use scoped review. The artist reviews descriptions of her practice and statement excerpts. The archive reviews record identifiers, institutional history, and claims about survey production. The union and speakers review quotation accuracy, context, naming, and sensitive framing. Conservation reviews only instructions that affect objects. The curator and editor retain responsibility for overall argument, length, and voice. Ask each reviewer to label comments factual correction, rights/permission, contextual concern, or preference. Factual and permission issues block; preferences are considered but do not confer whole-text veto.

Maintain a wording ledger with passage ID, current text, claimant, source, requested change, category, decision, rationale, and approver. When two factual authorities disagree, do not hide the conflict by choosing the smoother sentence. Identify the differing frames in the label if material, or narrow the claim to what the evidence supports. Freeze English on September 5, send one versioned file for Spanish translation, and route post-freeze changes through a bilingual change log so both languages remain aligned. Test printed hierarchy, line length, lighting, and reading distance before final production.

A practical scheduling constraint: fabrication has only four shop days available, September 21–24. The preparator can build the projection baffle, three tactile-map trays, two benches, and the passage graphic supports, but not if dimensions keep changing. Final wall measurements are due September 14. Large-print labels go to an outside printer with a seven-business-day turnaround. The media integrator is available September 28 and October 5, and the registrar wants all object installation completed before the second media day.

Can you create a dependency-aware production sequence through opening week, with a clear change-control rule? Include the November rotation preparation even though the physical swap occurs later. I need dates and owners, but not a recap of the choices that produced them.

Use September 14 as the geometry freeze. By that date, Inez and the preparator sign the measured wall, doorway, power, case, bench, baffle, tray, and passage-support dimensions. Any unknown is marked with a bounded tolerance; an unlabeled estimate is not a fabrication input.

September 5 remains English text freeze for translation. By September 11, the translator returns a first Spanish pass and the editor resolves questions with the relevant factual authority. September 14–16, design lays out bilingual standard and large-print labels against measured space. Send large-print files to the outside printer by September 17, allowing receipt and inspection before installation. Keep a corrected emergency file path, but do not rely on rush printing as ordinary schedule.

September 15–18, the preparator produces shop drawings and cut lists. Fabrication runs September 21–24 in this order: safety-critical baffle structure and supports, benches, tactile trays, then passage graphic supports. Inspect dimensions and edge finish at the end of each day so an early error does not consume all four days. Education receives trays for final handling checks on September 25.

On September 28, the media integrator installs power-safe hardware, player, projector, speakers, and cable management, then records a baseline four-hour test. No collection objects need be present. October 1–3, the registrar and preparator install cases and works under lender rules, with fragile works last after lighting is stable. Complete object installation and initial condition sign-off before October 5. On the second media day, load the sealed playback package, verify presets and recovery, measure light/heat/sound with objects protected, and hand the reset card to visitor services. October 6–9 covers labels, access review, route rehearsal, cleaning, and corrections that do not alter approved object handling. October 12–15 is staff training and opening readiness.

Change control: after geometry freeze, every proposed dimensional, material, media, or text change gets an ID, reason, affected dependencies, safety/rights assessment, cost, schedule impact, owner, and explicit approval. The preparator approves build feasibility, registrar conservation impact, editor bilingual text impact, and Inez final scope. No one changes a shop drawing or production file through informal chat.

Prepare November rotation materials during October installation: condition images, substitute-work inspection, packing map, alternate labels, wall coordinates, hardware list, reduced-object fallback, and delegate rule. Seal that packet after opening corrections and schedule a November 23 readiness check.

Visitor services tested the route with eighteen staff and found a queue at the passage whenever someone stopped to read the static graphic. We can keep the graphic, but it needs a short headline readable while moving and a longer version somewhere that does not narrow the route. They also found that the bench nearest the media room becomes an obstacle if it drifts more than ten centimetres from its floor marks. Facilities dislikes adhesive outlines on the wood floor.

Could you suggest a route-safe interpretation pattern and a reversible way to register the bench position? Add what front-line staff should observe during the first public weekend. Keep the answer focused on these operational findings.

Use the passage graphic as a glanceable threshold rather than a reading station. Limit it to one short headline, one date or scale cue if essential, and a directional visual that can be understood without stopping. Place the longer explanation immediately after the passage in a widened landing, duplicated in large print and available in the access guide. A small prompt can say that more detail is ahead; do not mount dense text at the narrowest point. Test the headline at walking pace from both directions and remove any element that causes readers to turn across opposing traffic.

For the bench, use reversible mechanical registration that does not adhere to the floor. Options include a thin custom spacer fixed to the bench's concealed underside that meets an existing wall base, or two low-profile stops attached to an approved freestanding weighted rail behind the bench. Facilities and conservation should inspect material, stability, cleaning access, trip risk, and whether the device changes the required wall clearance. If neither is safe, add lockable non-marking casters or feet specified by the preparator and use a daily measured placement from permanent architectural reference points. The ten-centimetre tolerance should become a maximum with a simpler target, such as two measured distances recorded on the opening checklist.

During the first weekend, front-line staff should sample rather than constantly intervene. At opening, midday, and the busiest hour, record whether visitors stop in the passage, direction of any queue, clear route width, mobility-device conflicts, group bunching, bench position, seated-view obstruction, and requests for the longer text. Note time and observed behavior without photographing identifiable visitors. Staff may invite people toward the wider reading point using neutral language; they should not move the bench without the assigned method or invent temporary floor markers.

Define escalation triggers: repeated passage blockage lasting more than a minute, inability to maintain the measured accessible route, bench movement beyond tolerance, or a near trip. Visitor services can deploy a trained person at the threshold as a temporary mitigation, but a persistent pattern returns to the exhibit team for graphic, group-entry, or furniture adjustment under change control.

We also need an opening-week incident card. Front-line staff should be able to respond to media failure, a visitor reporting distress about an oral-history excerpt, a spill in the lobby, or suspected object contact. They should not make rights decisions, conservation treatments, or public promises. The security desk has the registrar's and facilities manager's numbers; the curator is not always on site. We want one reporting form that can cover all four situations without encouraging staff to collect unnecessary personal information.

Please give me the response priorities and a compact common form. Finish with the unresolved approvals that remain across the project, so I can use them at tomorrow's cross-team meeting.

The shared priorities are people, collection, containment, escalation, and factual record—in that order, adjusted to the event.

For media failure, keep the route safe, activate the approved text-only fallback, note the health code, and contact the media duty person. Do not browse files or improvise a mix. For a visitor reporting distress, offer a quieter place, the route out, and available support such as seating or a companion; do not press for a personal account or debate the interpretation. Record only what the visitor volunteers and whether assistance was accepted. For a lobby spill, keep people away, call facilities, and protect the gallery threshold; staff should use only materials covered by their ordinary spill training. For suspected object contact, do not touch or reposition the object. Secure the immediate area, notify security and the registrar through the desk, preserve the observed conditions, and avoid accusing a visitor.

Use one form with: incident ID; date/time; staff name and location; category; immediate safety concern; brief observable facts; affected equipment/object area using its internal identifier; actions taken; fallback or barrier used; person contacted and time; service/area status; follow-up owner; and attachment references. Add an optional field for visitor contact information only if the visitor requests follow-up and consents. Do not record diagnoses, immigration or housing details, speculative blame, photographs of visitors, or full quoted testimony. Separate a direct short statement from staff interpretation.

Remaining approvals include lender sign-off on both rotation sets and delegate supervision; final oral-history excerpt/context and promotional-use boundaries; the union's credit order in proof; archive approval of its exact credit and survey context; September 12 tactile review and resulting changes; facilities/conservation approval of baffle, bench registration, and cable management; bilingual text proof; final measured geometry; media standard/quiet presets and failure fallback; security review of incident escalation; capacity and accessible-route sign-off; rights-safe tablet configuration; and the opening-week staffing roster. The cross-team meeting should assign an owner and deadline to each approval and identify which downstream production item stops if it is late.
